prompt: Many major museums hold objects that were removed from other countries in the past. Some people believe these objects should be returned to their countries of origin, while others argue they are better preserved and more widely seen where they are. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Two quite different arguments are usually made for keeping these objects where they are, and they deserve very different treatment. One is that the holding museums can look after them better. The other is that a single collection which places a Benin bronze near a Greek marble and a Tang burial figure lets a visitor see something that no national museum can show. The first argument was once true and mostly is not any more; the second is untouched by anything the restitution case says.

The claim for return is not really about heritage in the sentimental sense. It is about how the objects were obtained. A great many left during military occupation or under administrations the local population had no hand in choosing, and permission granted in those circumstances is not permission. There is a plainer inequity underneath as well: a Nigerian who wants to see the work of Nigerian craftsmen needs a visa, a flight and a hotel, while a Londoner walks in free on a wet Tuesday. No argument about conservation standards answers that.

It answered it once. Fifty years ago, some claimant countries genuinely lacked climate-controlled storage and trained conservators, and museums that said so were not merely being self-serving. But several have since built institutions to full international standard, in some cases specifically to receive what they are asking for, and a defence that was empirical has quietly turned into a habit. An argument that depended on a fact must be given up when the fact changes.

That leaves the universal collection, which is the serious objection and the one I would try to preserve. It does not, however, require ownership. Long loans in both directions, jointly curated exhibitions and shared conservation would keep the comparative displays that make those museums valuable while conceding the point about acquisition. The objects should return; the idea of a collection that lets a visitor see the whole world at once is worth keeping, and there is no reason it must be kept in the same place.
title: Should museums return what they hold?
